entry.title: Boring deploys are the goal
entry.summary: A good release is a non-event. Here is how small batches, automation and fast rollback make deploys boring, and what that looks like on a dashboard.
entry.content:
If your release is exciting, something is wrong. Nobody should clap when a deploy ends. Nobody should hold their breath while it runs.

I work in release engineering. My job is to make releases dull. I think this is the best compliment a deploy can get: "Did that already go out?"

#Why big releases hurt

A big release collects many changes. Each change is small and safe on its own. Together they are a pile that nobody can hold in their head.

When the pile breaks something, the question is "which change did it?" That question is slow to answer. You have a long diff, many authors, and a clock that runs while users wait.

Martin Fowler has a short note on this: when something is painful, do it more often. Pain pushes the team to make the step easier. Rare releases make the pain bigger and the habit weaker.

I have seen teams react to a bad release with more sign-offs and more meetings. I understand why. But I don't think it works. A manual sign-off asks a person to judge a huge change in an hour. That person cannot do it well. The ritual only moves the blame.

#Small batches do most of the work

The best tool I know is also the simplest. Ship less per deploy.

A deploy with one small change has a short list of suspects. If it fails, the cause is almost always that change. You find it in minutes, not hours. You also revert a small change with little fear.

This is why I say small changes are safe changes. It is not a slogan for me. It is how I decide where to spend time. I would rather make deploys cheap than make reviews longer.

Small batches ask for a few habits in the team:

  • Merge to the main branch often, in small pieces.
  • Keep unfinished work behind a switch, so it can ship but stay off.
  • Never let a change wait for a "release day".

#Automate the steps you fear

Pick the step in your release that makes people nervous. Often it is the step a person does by hand, from memory, once a week. Automate that step first.

A script does not forget the third item on the checklist. It does the same thing at 10:00 on Tuesday and at 17:45 on Friday. That is what I want from a release. The same result, every time.

Automation also makes the process visible. You can read it, review it and improve it. A hand-made process lives in one person's head, and that person goes on holiday.

I am not saying "remove all humans". People still decide what to ship and when to stop. But a person should not be the part that carries the steps. A person should be the part that checks the result.

#Make rollback the easy path

Every deploy needs a way back that is faster than the way forward.

The Google SRE book describes release engineering as a discipline of its own. One idea there matches my own view: releases should be repeatable and automated, so that nobody depends on one person's tricks.

Rollback puts this idea to the test. If going back means a long meeting, people will wait and hope. If going back means one command, people will use it early. Early rollback is cheap. Late rollback is a bad day.

Before any release I ask one question. "How do we undo this, and how long does it take?" If the answer is vague, the release is not ready. Database changes are the hard case here, because a schema change does not always revert as easily as code. I plan those in steps, and I will write about that in a later post.

#What boring looks like on a dashboard

A boring deploy has a clear signature in the data. The DORA research names four measures. How often you deploy. How long a change takes to reach production. How often a deploy fails. How fast you recover.

I look at them as a group. If I only watch speed, I may push teams to rush. If I only watch failures, I may push them to stop deploying. The healthy picture has many small deploys, a short wait from commit to production, few failures, and short recovery.

On a good day, the dashboard is flat and quiet. The deploy count goes up in small steps. The error line stays where it was. Nobody opens a channel for an incident.

That flat line is the goal. It looks like nothing happened. A lot of work went into making nothing happen.

#The hard part is not technical

I will be honest. The tools are not the main problem. Most teams I know can set up a pipeline.

The hard part is trust. A manager who has seen a bad release will ask for a gate. A developer who got blamed once will batch changes "to be safe". Both choices are human, and both make releases riskier.

So I spend as much time on blameless incident reviews as on pipelines. If a failure leads to blame, people hide risk. If it leads to a fix in the process, people ship smaller things, more often.

What is the most boring deploy you remember? Tell me. I like those stories.

entry.title: How I build side projects with AI: 7 rules that work
entry.summary: How I build real side projects with AI coding tools, and what I recommend. Keep the scope small, write the spec first, test everything, and stay the engineer.
entry.content:
I build side projects with AI tools. Three of them are live now. Migraine.Club is a migraine diary that makes summaries for doctors. Parley is a terminal app where AI investor personas debate a stock. Claude Life OS is a Claude skill for personal paperwork.

AI did not build these projects for me. It changed how I build them. Some things got much faster. Some things I now do more carefully than before.

Here are the seven rules that I follow. Each rule has what I do, and what I recommend to you.

#1. Start with a problem, not with a tool

I never start with "I want to build something with AI". I start with a problem that I, or people near me, have.

Migraine.Club started with one question. How can a person show their doctor clear data about their migraines? Every feature answers that question: the one-tap log, the doctor summary, and the dim mode for bad days.

My recommendation: write your problem in one sentence before you open any tool. When the problem is clear, the AI gets clear instructions. When the problem is not clear, the AI writes a lot of code that nobody needs.

#2. Write the spec before the prompt

AI is fast. A bad plan also becomes code fast.

Now I write a short spec before I ask for code. It is one page or less. It has four parts:

  • who the user is, and what their problem is,
  • what the feature must do,
  • what the feature must not do,
  • how I will know that it works.

Then I give the spec to the AI. The result is much better. And I have something to check the result against.

My recommendation: keep the specs in the repository, next to the code. The next prompt can use them too.

#3. Keep each task small

I give the AI one small task at a time. "Add a button that exports the last 30 days as a PDF" is a good task. "Build the reports module" is not a good task.

Small tasks give small diffs. I can read a small diff in two minutes. Nobody really reads a diff with 2,000 lines. That is how bugs get into production.

My recommendation: if you cannot describe the task in two sentences, split it. Release engineering taught me the same rule. Small changes are safe changes.

#4. You are still the engineer

The AI writes the code. I own the code.

I read every diff. I run it. I ask "why?" when something looks strange. If I cannot explain a piece of code, I do not merge it.

AI sounds very sure, also when it is wrong. It can use an API that does not exist. It can remove a check "to make the code simpler".

My recommendation: review AI code like code from a new colleague. Be friendly, but check everything. You are the last check before your users.

#5. Let the tests decide

For me, tests are the best way to agree with an AI about what "correct" means.

I ask for the tests first, or together with the code. Then I run them. When a test fails, I give the error output back to the AI. This loop is fast and honest. A test does not care how sure the answer sounds.

This is very important in Migraine.Club. The app shows scores like HIT-6 and MIDAS. A wrong score is worse than no score.

My recommendation: everything that calculates or stores data needs tests with known inputs and known results, before real people see it.

#6. Make the hard decisions yourself

Some decisions are not for the AI: privacy, security, the data model, and what the product promises to its users.

Migraine.Club is privacy-first. I made that decision on day one, and it shaped everything after it. Parley is local-first for a similar reason. A tool does not know what your users trust you with.

My recommendation: write these decisions in your spec as rules. Then the AI follows them, and you can see quickly when it does not.

#7. Ship early, then make it better

A side project that is not online helps nobody. I put a first version live as soon as it does one thing well.

Real users show you what is important. Usually it is not what you expected. Parley is a terminal app. It does not need a website to be useful.

My recommendation: pick the smallest form that works. A small web app or a command-line tool is enough for version one.

#What AI changed for me

Before AI tools, my side projects often stopped in the boring middle part. Forms, settings pages, configuration, glue code. Now that part takes evenings, not weeks.

So my time goes to the parts that matter: the problem, the decisions and the review.

I think of AI as a very fast junior colleague. I give it clear tasks. I check its work. I keep the responsibility.

#My checklist

  • One problem, in one sentence.
  • A one-page spec before the first prompt.
  • One small task per prompt.
  • Read and run every diff.
  • Tests for everything that calculates or stores data.
  • Privacy and security decisions made by you.
  • A live first version, as early as possible.

Do you build something with AI in your free time? Tell me about it. I read every message.
